overview:
Kublai Khan, grandson of Chinggis Khan, declared a Chinese-style dynastic name for his realm in 1271, taking "Great Yuan" from a phrase in the Book of Changes meaning primal origin. He had already won a civil war against his brother Ariq Böke for the title of Great Khan, and the cost of that fight was that the western Mongol khanates drifted into effective independence; the Yuan claimed seniority over them but ruled only the eastern half of what Chinggis had assembled. Kublai built a new capital, Dadu, on the site of present-day Beijing, kept Shangdu in the steppe as a summer seat, and finished the long grinding war against the Southern Song, whose last resistance ended at sea in 1279. For the first time in three centuries north and south China were under one government, and for the first time ever the whole of it was ruled by a conquest regime from outside.

Governing it meant compromise. The Yuan kept the outward furniture of Chinese administration — ministries, provinces, a census, a tax system — while reserving decisive posts for Mongols and for Semu, the Central Asian, Turkic, Persian and other non-Chinese servants of the throne who ran much of the fiscal machinery. The civil service examinations, the ladder by which Chinese literati had traditionally climbed, were suspended for decades and only revived in the 1310s, and even then filled a small share of offices. Later Chinese tradition described a rigid four-tier ranking of Mongols, Semu, northern Chinese and southern Chinese; recent scholarship, working from household registration documents, argues the scheme was never codified quite that neatly, though legal and fiscal discrimination by group certainly existed. Displaced scholars turned to painting, private study and the theatre, and Yuan drama and literati landscape painting became two of the most admired bodies of work in Chinese art. The empire was also unusually porous: Tibetan Buddhist clergy held high favour, the Phags-pa script was commissioned to write the empire's several languages, Muslim astronomers and engineers worked at court, and merchants and envoys moved along routes that carried Marco Polo east and Chinese porcelain and paper money west.

The fourteenth century went badly. Succession fights put nine emperors on the throne in the twenty-six years after 1307, overissue of paper currency drove inflation, and the fiscal base narrowed while spending did not. Cold, drought, epidemic and repeated Yellow River flooding hit hardest in the 1330s and 1340s; a vast conscripted labour project to redirect the river in 1351 helped touch off the Red Turban risings, a mix of millenarian White Lotus religion and rural desperation. Regional warlords, some nominally loyal, fought each other as much as the throne. Zhu Yuanzhang, a former monk and beggar who rose through the rebel armies, took the Yangtze region and then sent forces north; in 1368 the last Yuan emperor, Toghon Temür, abandoned Dadu for the steppe rather than fight for it. He and his successors ruled on in Mongolia as what historians call the Northern Yuan, while Zhu founded the Ming.
significance: The Yuan set the terms for everything that followed in China's imperial history. It reunified a country divided since the tenth century and fixed Beijing as the capital, a choice the Ming and Qing inherited and modern China kept. It normalised the idea that a non-Han house could hold the Mandate of Heaven, a precedent the Manchus would lean on four centuries later, and it left the Ming founder with a lasting anxiety about steppe frontiers that shaped Chinese defence policy for two hundred years. Its openness to the wider Eurasian world — the flow of astronomers, artisans, drugs, maps, tax farmers and travellers across the Mongol domains — gave Europe its most detailed picture of China before the sixteenth century and moved technologies and goods in both directions. And its collapse remains one of history's clearest cases of a state undone less by conquest than by compounding stress: monetary failure, ecological disaster and a ruling elite too busy with its own succession quarrels to respond.
coverage: Written from reference summaries — Wikipedia, Britannica, the Met's art-historical essay, World History Encyclopedia — plus a note of Funada Yoshiyuki's revisionist work on the four-class system; the dataset itself holds no mappable events beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to a place or date the map can display. The wider record is also uneven: the official Yuan History was compiled hastily by Ming scholars hostile to the dynasty they had overthrown, Mongol-language and Persian sources give a different and less integrated picture than the Chinese ones, and basic questions — how far Mongol rule was "sinicised," how severe the population loss of the fourteenth century really was, whether the ethnic ranking was law or later shorthand — remain genuinely open.
